The war cost Italy 1.3 billion lire, nearly a billion more than Giovanni Giolitti estimated before the war. This ruined ten years of fiscal prudence.

Jacobite rising of 1745.aftermath: upright=0.8|alt=Lord Lovat by Hogarth| Lovat, sketched by William Hogarth at St Albans, on his way to London for trial and later execution

January Uprising.aftermath:
Wounded insurgent, by Stanisław Witkiewicz, 1881
These measures of cultural eradication proved to be only partially effective. In 1905, 41 years after Russia crushed the uprising, the next generation of Poles rose once again in the Łódź insurrection, which too failed.
January Uprising.outcome: Russian victory; revolt suppressed by spring 1864.

Java War.aftermath:
Grave of Diponegoro and his wife in Makassar
Diponegoro was exiled to Manado with a number of followers, as colonial authorities saw that keeping him in Java posed an unacceptable risk. He was moved to the more fortified Makassar in 1833 due to concerns of a British attack on Manado in the event of a European conflict – the Dutch feared that Diponegoro with British support might lead another revolt in Java. Diponegoro would be restricted to Fort Rotterdam starting in 1849, and he died on 8 January 1855. Sentot was given command of a Javanese unit and took part in the Padri War, but was then exiled to Bengkulu in 1833.
Java War.outcome: Dutch victory; Prince Diponegoro exiled, Java pacified by 1830.

Jin–Song wars.aftermath: A century and a half of war between the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty and Song China. The Jin conquered the Northern Song heartland (Jingkang Incident, 1127) and drove the survivors south of the Huai. The Mongol invasion of 1232-1234 ultimately destroyed the Jin; the Southern Song held out until 1279.

Khmelnytsky Uprising.aftermath: The uprising is generally considered to have resulted in success or Cossack victory, as it achieved its main goals of ending Polish–Lithuanian rule over much of the Ukrainian lands and establishing the Cossack Hetmanate. However, the Cossacks' struggle to consolidate their victory, increasing external pressures, and internal divisions after Khmelnytsky's death led to instability and decline for his state during the post-uprising period. This period in Ukrainian history is known as the Ruin.

King George's War.outcome: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, Status quo ante bellum
King George's War.aftermath:
British soldiers guarding Halifax in 1749. Fighting in Nova Scotia between the British, and the Acadian and Mi'kmaq militias continued even after the signing of the peace treaty.
The war took a heavy toll, especially in the northern British colonies. The losses of Massachusetts men alone in 1745–46 have been estimated as 8% of that colony's adult male population.

King Philip's War.outcome: New England Confederation victory, Wabanaki victory in Maine
King Philip's War.aftermath:
Southern New England
The war in southern New England largely ended with Metacom's death. More than 1,000 colonists and 3,000 Natives had died. Hundreds of Native captives were enslaved. Some women and children were sold as indentured servants or slaves to the households of English settlers, but the majority, including Metacom's son and most adult men, were transported to slave markets in Bermuda, Barbados, Jamaica, Spain, Portugal, Madeira, and the Azores. Other survivors joined western and northern tribes and refugee communities as captives or tribal members. Some of the Native refugees returned to southern New England. The Narragansetts, Wampanoags, Podunks, Nipmucks suffered substantial losses, several smaller bands were virtually eliminated as organized bands.

King William's War.outcome: Peace of Ryswick, Status quo ante bellum
King William's War.aftermath: The Treaty of Ryswick, signed in September 1697 ended the war between the two colonial powers and reverted the colonial borders to the status quo ante bellum. The peace did not last long. and within five years, the colonies were embroiled in the next phase of the colonial wars, Queen Anne's War. After their settlement with France in 1701, the Iroquois remained neutral in that conflict and never took part in active hostilities against either side.

Korean War.outcome: Korean Armistice Agreement (27 July 1953) suspended fighting along a line near the original 38th parallel. No peace treaty has ever been signed. The war ended in stalemate.
Korean War.aftermath: Korea remained divided between the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in the north and the Republic of Korea in the south. The Korean Demilitarized Zone runs roughly along the ceasefire line. ~3 million people died, most of them civilians. The war hardened the Cold War alliance system and brought the United States into a permanent military presence in East Asia.
Korean War.keyTerms: Armistice signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 between the United Nations Command, North Korea, and the Chinese People's Volunteer Army. South Korea refused to sign.
notable: Permanent division of Korea at the Demilitarized Zone
First major proxy war of the Cold War
United States military presence in South Korea continues to the present
Technically still a state of war, not peace

Kosovo War.outcome: NATO-KLA victory; Kumanovo Agreement (June 1999) ends Serbian rule.
Kosovo War.aftermath: Eighteen months of war in Kosovo capped by 78 days of NATO bombing of Yugoslavia. Slobodan Milošević withdrew Serbian forces; Kosovo passed under UN administration. Kosovo declared independence in 2008 — recognised by most of the West but not by Russia, China, or several EU states.

Kościuszko Uprising.aftermath:
The uprising was bloodily suppressed, the Polish rebels lost 27,000 men and the Russians 4,080.
After the failure of the Kościuszko Uprising, Poland ceased to exist for 123 years, and all of its institutions were gradually banned by the partitioning powers. However, the uprising also marked the start of modern political thought in Poland and Central Europe. Kościuszko's Proclamation of Połaniec and the radical leftist Jacobins started the Polish leftist movement. Many prominent Polish politicians who were active during the uprising became the backbone of Polish politics, both at home and abroad, in the 19th century.

Kumul Rebellion.aftermath: A five-year revolt (1931-1934) by the Uyghur population of Kumul (Hami) against the Han Chinese governor of Xinjiang. The rebellion drew in Hui Muslim forces under Ma Zhongying and Soviet intervention; it ended with Sheng Shicai's pro-Soviet regime taking control of Xinjiang.

Lamian War.aftermath:
Athens' punishment
Bust of Demosthenes in the Louvre. Demosthenes committed suicide to avoid his capture by Macedonia.
Once Antipater reached Boeotia, Athens sought for peace. The Athenian delegation to Antipater was composed of Demades and Phocion, the two leading politician who had spoken against the war with Macedonia, as well as Xenocrates of Chalcedon, the head of Plato's Academy. Antipater demanded the installation of a Macedonian garrison in the fortress of Munychia in the harbour of Piraeus, which was thus taken on 18 September 322 BC.

Lebanese Civil War.aftermath:
Post-conflict Syrian occupation
The post-war occupation of the country by the Syrian Arab Republic was particularly politically disadvantageous to the Maronite population, as most of their leadership was driven into exile, or had been assassinated or jailed.
Lebanese Civil War.outcome: Taif Agreement (1989) and Syrian-led settlement end fifteen years of war.

Libyan civil war (2014–2020).aftermath: Six years of war between the Tobruk-based House of Representatives (backed by the LNA under Khalifa Haftar) and the Tripoli-based GNA. Foreign intervention (Russia, Turkey, UAE, Egypt) intensified the war. The October 2020 ceasefire and Berlin Conference framework produced a fragile transitional process.

Lithuanian Civil War (1432–1438).aftermath: Švitrigaila was losing his influence in the Slavic principalities and could no longer resist Poland and Sigismund Kęstutaitis. On 4 September 1437, he attempted to reconcile with Poland: he would rule the lands that still backed him (chiefly Kiev and Volhynia), and after his death these territories would pass to the King of Poland. However, under strong protest from Sigismund, the Polish Senate declined to ratify the treaty. In 1438 Švitrigaila withdrew to Moldavia.}} The reign of Sigismund Kęstutaitis was brief, he was assassinated in 1440. Švitrigaila returned from exile in 1442 and ruled Lutsk until his death a decade later.
Lithuanian Civil War (1432–1438).outcome: Victory for Sigismund Kęstutaitis with Polish backing.

Lithuanian Crusade.outcome: Inconclusive; Lithuania accepted Christianity in 1387, ending the crusading rationale.
Lithuanian Crusade.aftermath: Two centuries of Teutonic Order campaigns against pagan Lithuania. The dynastic union of Lithuania and Poland (Krewo 1385) and the conversion of Jogaila in 1387 ended the religious pretext; the Order's defeat at Tannenberg (1410) ended its military dominance.

Livonian Crusade.aftermath:
Territories controlled by the Teutonic Order in 1410
In 1227 the Livonian Brothers of the Sword conquered all Danish territories in Northern Estonia. After the Battle of Saule the surviving members of the Brothers of the Sword merged into the Teutonic Order of Prussia in 1237 and became known as Livonian Order. On 7 June 1238, by the Treaty of Stensby, the Teutonic knights returned the Duchy of Estonia to Valdemar II, until in 1346, after St. George's Night Uprising, the lands were sold back to the order and became part of the Ordensstaat.
Livonian Crusade.outcome: Crusader victory; Baltic pagans converted, Livonian Order established.

Livonian War.aftermath: The post-war Duchy of Courland and Semigallia south of the Düna (Daugava) river experienced a period of political stability based on the 1561 Treaty of Vilnius, later modified by the 1617 Formula regiminis and Statuta Curlandiæ, which granted indigenous nobles additional rights at the duke's expense. North of the Düna, Báthory reduced the privileges Sigismund had granted the Duchy of Livonia, regarding the regained territories as the spoils of war. Polish gradually replaced German as the administrative language and the establishment of voivodeships reduced the Baltic German administration.
Livonian War.keyTerms: Truce of Yam-Zapolsky (January 15, 1582); Truce of Plussa (1583)

Long Turkish War.aftermath: The Long War ended with the Peace of Zsitvatorok on November 11, 1606, with meagre territorial gains for the two main empiresthe Ottomans won the fortresses of Eger, and Kanizsa, but gave the region of Vác (which they had occupied since 1541) to Austria. The treaty confirmed the Ottomans' inability to penetrate further into Habsburg territories. It also demonstrated that Transylvania was beyond Habsburg power. Although Emperor Rudolf had failed in his war objectives, he nonetheless won some prestige thanks to this resistance to the Ottomans, by presenting the war as a victory. The sultan acknowledged his status as an equal and the treaty stabilized conditions on the Habsburg–Ottoman frontier. Also, Stephen Bocskai managed to retain his independence.

Lower Canada Rebellion.aftermath:
The green, white, and red tricolour used by the between 1832 and 1838.]]
After the first insurrection, the Pied-du-Courant Prison in Montreal was overfull. In July, Durham emptied it. When hostilities resumed in 1838, the prison filled with even more prisoners. Martial law was declared. This allowed the government to imprison people without reason. Ninety-nine prisoners from the second rebellion were sentenced to death. Twelve were hanged. the last hanging is dramatized in the 2001 film February 15, 1839. The government feared that the populace would sympathize with the prisoners. So, 141 prisoners from Lower and Upper Canada were instead sent to work camps in Australia.

Maccabean Revolt.aftermath:
alt=Topographic map of Palestine at the start of the Hasmonean dynasty|Topographic map of the southern Levant at the start of the Hasmonean dynasty

In 135 BCE, Simon and two of his sons (Mattathias and Judas) were murdered by his son-in-law, Ptolemy son of Abubus, at a feast in Jericho. All five sons of Mattathias were now gone with Simon joining his brothers in death, leaving leadership to the next generation. Simon's third son, John Hyrcanus, became High Priest of Israel. King Antiochus VII would personally invade and besiege Jerusalem in 134 BCE, but after Hyrcanus paid a ransom and ceded the cities of Joppa and Gazara, the Seleucids left peacefully.
Maccabean Revolt.outcome: Maccabean victory; Hasmonean dynasty established, Jerusalem Temple rededicated.

Macedonian Struggle.aftermath:
The success of Greek efforts in Macedonia was an experience that gave confidence to the country. It helped develop an intention to annex Greek-speaking areas, and bolster Greek presence in the still Ottoman ruled Macedonia.
 
The events in Macedonia, specifically the consequences of the conflicts between Greek and Bulgarian national activists, including Greek massacres against the Bulgarian population in 1905 and 1906, gave rise to pogroms against the ca. 70,000–80,000-strong Greek communities that lived in Bulgaria, who were considered to share responsibility for the actions of the Greek guerrilla groups.
Macedonian Struggle.outcome: Inconclusive; the Balkan Wars (1912-1913) supersede and partition Ottoman Macedonia.

Mahdist War.aftermath: The British set up a new colonial system, the Anglo-Egyptian administration, which effectively established British domination over Sudan. This ended with the independence of Sudan in 1956. The Tukrir sided with the Mahdists during their war against Ethiopia and disappeared with their defeat.
Mahdist War.outcome: Anglo-Egyptian victory at Omdurman (1898); Mahdist state extinguished.

Mali War.outcome: Ongoing; Tuareg-Islamist offensive of 2012 reversed by French intervention but jihadist insurgency continues.
Mali War.aftermath: A decade-long war that began with the 2012 Tuareg revolt and the AQIM/Ansar Dine takeover of northern Mali. French Operation Serval (2013) and the EU/UN missions stabilised the south but the insurgency mutated. Wagner Group replaced French forces in 2022.

Mauritius campaign of 1809–1811.aftermath: The fall of Isle de France marked the end of the active British campaign and saw six frigates and over 200 cannon fall into British hands, in addition to the island itself, which was returned to its original Dutch name of Mauritius, and has been known as such ever since. The island remained under British control until granted independence in 1968. The British forces in the region were scaled back, command passing to Beaver, who sent ships to eliminate French ports on Madagascar and in the Seychelles.

Mercenary War.aftermath: The Romans required a strong military presence on Sardinia and Corsica for at least the next seven years, as they struggled to suppress the local inhabitants. The seizure of Sardinia and Corsica by Rome and the additional indemnity fuelled resentment in Carthage. Polybius considered this act of bad faith by the Romans to be the single greatest cause of war with Carthage breaking out again nineteen years later. The role of Hamilcar Barca in the victory greatly enhanced the prestige and power of the Barcid family. Immediately after the war, Hamilcar led many of his veterans on an expedition to expand Carthaginian holdings in southern Iberia. this was to become a semi-autonomous Barcid fiefdom.

Mexican War of Independence.aftermath: Flag of the Mexican Empire of Iturbide, the template for the modern Mexican flag with the eagle perched on a cactus. The crown on the eagle's head symbolizes monarchy in Mexico.

Middle Eastern theatre of World War I.aftermath: On 30 October 1918, the Armistice of Mudros was signed aboard in Mudros port on the island of Lemnos between the Ottoman Empire and the Triple Entente. Ottoman operations in the active combat theatres ceased.

Moldavian Magnate Wars.outcome: Ottoman victory; Polish magnate interventions checked.
Moldavian Magnate Wars.aftermath: Three decades of war between Polish magnates and the Ottoman Empire over the Moldavian throne. The Polish defeats accelerated the breakdown of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth's ability to project power east and south.

Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus'.aftermath:
Carpine's account
The Ystoria Mongalorum, written by Italian diplomat Giovanni da Pian del Carpine () in Latin just after he visited Kiev in 1246, contains a brief passage mentioning the siege of Kiev that happened several years earlier. Although frequently cited by earlier historians, the accuracy of this account has been questioned, especially because the passage from the first redaction of Carpini's manuscript copies was substantially expanded in the second redaction, which breaks the narrative of the first, and partially contradicts it.
{| class="wikitable"! width="50%" | First redaction of Carpini's Ystoria Mongalorum!

Mongol invasions of India.aftermath: A century of Mongol and Chagatai raids into the Indus valley and northern India. The Delhi Sultanate under the Khaljis and Tughluqs repelled the major invasions, including the catastrophic Mongol defeat at Amroha (1305). The Mongol threat shaped Delhi Sultanate fortifications and military organisation for generations.

Montenotte campaign.aftermath: Succeeding where earlier armies had failed, Bonaparte and his soldiers knocked Sardinia out of the war in a single brief campaign. The French suffered 6,000 casualties during the campaign. Total Austrian and Sardinian losses stood around 25,000. With Sardinia-Piedmont pacified, the French were free to direct their attentions on their major enemy, Austria. Soon Bonaparte launched a new offensive, which resulted in victories over Beaulieu at the battles of Fombio and Lodi in May.

Morean War.aftermath:
Venetian four-zecchino coin celebrating the Treaty of Karlowitz
The Treaty of Karlowitz, signed in January 1699, confirmed the Venetian possession of Kephalonia, and the Morea with the island of Aigina, which became organized as the "Kingdom of the Morea" (), divided into four provinces: Romania, with seat at Nafplion (Napoli di Romania), Laconia, with seat at Monemvasia (Malvasia), Messenia, with seat at Navarino, and Achaea, with seat at Patras (Patrasso). The war had created a demographic and economic crisis in the Peloponnese. According to the first census conducted by the Venetians, there were 86,468 people in the peninsula compared to a pre-war population of around 200,000.

Moro Rebellion.aftermath: A decade-long insurgency against US colonial rule in the southern Philippines. American forces conducted brutal campaigns including the Battles of Bud Dajo (1906) and Bud Bagsak (1913). The conflict produced the .45 ACP cartridge and pacification methods later applied in counter-insurgency campaigns globally.

Moro conflict.outcome: Ongoing as of late 2025; 2014 Bangsamoro Framework Agreement and 2018 BOL produced the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region.
Moro conflict.aftermath: A half-century of insurgency in the southern Philippines by Moro National Liberation Front and Moro Islamic Liberation Front, complicated by Abu Sayyaf and ISIS-affiliated factions. 120,000 dead; the 2014 framework agreement produced the Bangsamoro autonomous region in 2019.

Moroccan–Portuguese conflicts.aftermath: Five years after the recapture of Mazagan, in 1774, the Governments of Morocco and Portugal concluded a Peace and Friendship Agreement, one of the oldest bilateral agreements of both nations.

Muslim conquest of Persia.keyTerms: Battle of al-Qādisiyyah (November 636); Battle of Nahavand (641)
Muslim conquest of Persia.aftermath: A two-decade campaign (633-654) that destroyed the Sasanian Empire and brought the Iranian plateau into the Caliphate. Yazdegerd III's death at Merv (651) ended Sasanian resistance. The conquest produced the long Iranian Islamic civilisation — and a Persian cultural continuity that ultimately reshaped Islamic civilisation itself.

Muslim conquest of Transoxiana.aftermath: A four-decade campaign (705-751) that brought Central Asia between the Oxus and Jaxartes into the Umayyad Caliphate. The Arab victory over Tang China at Talas (751) confirmed Muslim dominance in Transoxiana and shaped the Islamic-Chinese frontier for centuries.

Muslim–Quraysh War.aftermath: Eight years (622-630) of war between the Muslim community at Medina and the Quraysh of Mecca. The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628) and the conquest of Mecca (630) ended the war with the conversion of the Quraysh and the unification of Arabia under Islam.

Napoleonic Wars.outcome: Decisive Coalition victory at Waterloo (18 June 1815) ended Napoleon's Hundred Days. The Seventh Coalition (United Kingdom, Prussia, Austria, Russia, and others) won.
Napoleonic Wars.aftermath: Napoleon abdicated and was exiled to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821. The Congress of Vienna (1814 to 1815) redrew the map of Europe and restored the Bourbon monarchy in France. The Concert of Europe held off general European war for nearly a century. Roughly 3.5 to 6 million people died across two decades of conflict. Spanish American colonies, weakened by the long war, broke away over the following decade.
Napoleonic Wars.keyTerms: Treaty of Paris (1815) and the Congress of Vienna's Final Act (9 June 1815).
notable: Restoration of the Bourbons in France
Creation of the German Confederation
Loss of most Spanish colonies in the Americas over the next decade
Foundation of the post-1815 Concert of Europe

Neapolitan War.aftermath: Shortly after the end of the war, the Kingdoms of Naples and Sicily were finally united to create the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Although the two kingdoms had been ruled by the same king since 1721, the formal union did not happen until 1816. King Ferdinand IV of Naples and III of Sicily would become King Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies. Meanwhile, the Austrians consolidated their gains in Northern Italy into the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia.
Neapolitan War.outcome: Austrian victory; Bourbon restoration in Naples (May 1815).

New Guinea campaign.aftermath: A four-year campaign (1942-1945) in which Australian and American forces fought one of the longest and grimmest Pacific theatres of WWII against the Japanese 18th Army. The Kokoda Track campaign halted the Japanese drive on Port Moresby; the eventual reconquest cut off and bypassed major Japanese garrisons.

New York and New Jersey campaign.aftermath: A six-month (July 1776 - January 1777) campaign in which the British army drove Washington's Continental Army out of New York and across New Jersey. Washington's counterstrokes at Trenton (December 1776) and Princeton (January 1777) saved the Revolution from collapse during its lowest point.

Nez Perce War.aftermath:
The Nez Perce prisoners arrive at the Tongue River Cantonment on October 23.
In total, the Nez Perce engaged 2,000 American soldiers of different military units, as well as their Indian auxiliaries. They fought "eighteen engagements, including four major battles and at least four fiercely contested skirmishes." Many people praised the Nez Perce for their exemplary conduct and skilled fighting ability. The Montana newspaper New North-West stated: "Their warfare since they entered Montana has been almost universally marked so far by the highest characteristics recognized by civilized nations. "

North-West Rebellion.aftermath: The end of the conflict led to the trial of Louis Riel, a trial that sparked national controversy between English and French Canada.The conflict was Canada's first independent military action. It cost about $5 million. Although it lost the Conservative Party most of its support in Quebec, at least temporarily, it secured anglophone control of the Prairies (following the Rebellion, no First Nations politician became premier until Wab Kinew in 2023). It also demonstrated the Canadian government was capable of decisive action.

Northern Seven Years' War.outcome: See Peace negotiations and consequences, {{Collapsible list|bullets=yes|title=Full results|Treaty of Stettin (1570)
Northern Seven Years' War.aftermath: Seven years of war (1563-1570) between Sweden and a Danish-Polish-Lübeck coalition. The Treaty of Stettin restored pre-war borders; the war's real impact was financial exhaustion that shaped subsequent Baltic politics for a generation.

Northwest Indian War.aftermath: Fort Lernoult and Fort Miami were abandoned by the British in 1796 as a condition of the Jay Treaty. After two decades of efforts to take Detroit, U.S. forces under Colonel Hamtramck occupied Fort Lernoult the next day. The U.S. renamed Fort Lernoult to Fort Detroit and abandoned Fort Miami in 1799. The British re-captured Fort Detroit and Fort Miami during the War of 1812. Fort Detroit was abandoned one year later as American forces advanced towards it, and Fort Miami was abandoned in 1814 and eventually demolished.

November Uprising.aftermath:
Lithuanian Litas commemorative coin dedicated to the uprising
A Polish 2 zloty coin from the Uprising
Relics of the uprising of 1831, exhibited in the National Museum of Lithuania in Vilnius.
November Uprising.outcome: Russian victory; Congress Poland's constitution revoked, Russian rule tightened.

Ottoman–Habsburg wars.aftermath: Three centuries (1526-1791) of intermittent war between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires for control of Hungary and the Balkans. The Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) marked the strategic turning point — the first major Ottoman territorial cession. The wars shaped the demographic and religious geography of central Europe.

Ottoman–Persian War (1505–1517).aftermath: Following these battles and campaigns, the Ottomans secured control over Eastern Anatolia and northern Iraq (including Mosul).

Ottoman–Safavid War (1578–1590).aftermath:
Ottoman troops under Lala Mustafa Pasha, and Alexander II of Kakheti with his Georgian troops (bottom) at the conquest of Sheki in Shirvan from the Safavids on 10 September 1578. Nusretname, Topkapi, H.1365
A peace of Constantinople was concluded on 21 March 1590, in which the Safavids were forced to confirm these Ottoman conquests, as well as promising to end Shiite propaganda in Ottoman territories and persecution of Sunnis in its own lands. By ceding many of its integral regions to the Ottomans, Abbas could settle matters in his crumbling state first, which had been neglected for so long by his father Mohammad Khodabanda.

Pacific War.outcome: Surrender of Japan (2 September 1945) aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. The Allies (United States, China, United Kingdom, Australia, and others) won.
Pacific War.aftermath: Japan was occupied by the United States under General Douglas MacArthur until 1952, with a new constitution and demilitarization imposed. Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria, and other Japanese-held territories were returned or transferred to other powers. The atomic bombings of Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August) ended the war and opened the nuclear age. China resumed its civil war between Nationalists and Communists, won by the Communists in 1949.
Pacific War.keyTerms: Instrument of Surrender of Japan signed aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, 2 September 1945.
notable: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
United States occupation and democratization of Japan
Independence movements in Korea, Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines
Chinese Civil War resumes, won by Mao Zedong in 1949

Paraguay campaign.aftermath: The Paraguay campaign was a complete defeat for the Primera Junta from a military point of view. For Paraguay, the defeat of Belgrano resulted in independence from Buenos Aires, and was followed for independence from Spain. Paraguay and Buenos Aires maintained good relationships later, thoug not being part of the same political entity anymore.

Paraguayan War.aftermath: Six years of war (1864-1870) between Paraguay and the Triple Alliance of Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay. The war destroyed Paraguay — perhaps 60-70% of the male population killed, the country reduced to subsistence. Brazil and Argentina dominated the Río de la Plata for decades afterward.

Paris Commune.aftermath: Two months (March-May 1871) of revolutionary government in Paris after the French defeat at Sedan. The Versailles army's May 1871 reconquest of the city (Semaine sanglante) killed approximately 20,000 Communards. The Commune became a foundational reference for revolutionary socialism — invoked by Marx, Lenin, and Mao.

Peloponnesian War.aftermath: The overall effect of the war in Greece proper was to replace the Athenian Empire with a Spartan empire. After the battle of Aegospotami, Sparta took over the Athenian empire and kept all its tribute revenues for itself, starting its own hegemony. Sparta's allies, who had made greater sacrifices in the war than had Sparta, got nothing.

Peninsular War.aftermath: upright=0.9|alt=Napoleon on the island of Elba.|Horace Vernet: Napoleon on the Island of Elba Awaiting the brig Inconstant. (1863)
Peninsular War.keyTerms: Battle of Vitoria (June 21, 1813); Battle of Toulouse (April 10, 1814)
Peninsular War.outcome: Anglo-Spanish-Portuguese victory; French forces driven out of Spain by 1814.

Peruvian War of Independence.aftermath: The independence of Peru was an important chapter in the Hispano-American wars of independence. Spain renounced all their continental American territories ten years later in 1836 leaving very little of its vast empire intact.
Peruvian War of Independence.outcome: Patriot victory; Spanish forces defeated at Ayacucho (December 1824).

Philippine Revolution.aftermath: A two-year revolution against Spanish rule that ended with the Spanish capitulation in Manila during the Spanish–American War. The First Philippine Republic, proclaimed at Malolos, would fight the next war against the United States.

Philippine–American War.aftermath:
Postwar conflicts
After military rule was terminated on July 4, 1901, the Philippine Constabulary was established as an archipelago-wide police force to control brigandage and deal with the remnants of the Republic. Organized and initially commanded by Brigadier General Henry Tureman Allen, the Philippine Constabulary gradually took responsibility for suppressing hostile forces' activities. Remnants of Aguinaldo's Republic, and remnants or holdovers of the Katipunan organization, which had predated the American presence, and other resistance groups all remained active, fighting for nearly a decade after the official end of the war.
Philippine–American War.outcome: US victory; First Philippine Republic dissolved 1902, Moro Rebellion continues to 1913.

Phyle Campaign.aftermath: Lysander's faction at Sparta was furious and along with King Agis brought Pausanias to trial to the end of 403 BCE. The exact charge is uncertain but the essence was presumably that he had been soft on Athens. Fifteen of the Gerousia, including Agis, voted guilty, but fourteen Gerousia, as well as all five Ephors, voted not guilty so he was acquitted.
Phyle Campaign.outcome: Democratic victory; Thirty Tyrants overthrown, Athenian democracy restored 403 BC.

Polish–Cossack–Tatar War (1666–1671).aftermath: Five years of war between Poland-Lithuania and a Cossack-Tatar alliance over right-bank Ukraine. The war ended inconclusively with the Treaty of Buchach (1672) and the larger Polish-Ottoman war that followed.

Polish–Russian War of 1792.aftermath: Most Polish historians agree that the Polish capitulation was a mistake both from the military perspective, and the political one. In the realm of military, the Poles had reasonable chances to defend the Vistula river line, and exhaust the Russian invading forces. From the political one, showing a willingness to fight could have persuaded the partitioning powers that their plan was too costly.

Polish–Soviet War.aftermath: 'The Miracle at the Vistula' — Piłsudski's August 1920 counter-attack outside Warsaw — halted the Red Army's westward march and saved Polish independence for nineteen years. The eastern lands Poland kept were lost again in 1939 and never returned.

Polish–Swedish War (1600–1611).aftermath: The result of the war is disputed among historians. Some historians, like Edgar Kiser, Kriss A. Drass, and William Brustein, claim that the outcome of the war was "even", while other historians, like Andrej Kotljarchuk, claim that the war was a Polish–Lithuanian military success.

Polish–Swedish War (1626–1629).aftermath: During the final phase of this conflict, there was a Franco-Dutch-Swedish diplomatic activity from 1627 until 1635, envoys Louis Deshayes, Cornelius Haga, Antoni Monier, Johan Müller, Paul Strassburg and Jacques Roussel) in an effort to form an Anti-Catholic coalition in the west with the Eastern Orthodox Church and Muslims by inviting the Russia, the Zaporozhian Cossacks, Crimean Khanate, Transylvania, Moldavia, Wallachia and the Ottoman Empire as allies.

Pontiac's War.outcome: Military stalemate, with negotiated policy concessions in favor of the Native American side
Pontiac's War.aftermath: Because many white children taken as captives had been adopted into Native families, their forced return often resulted in emotional scenes, as depicted in this engraving based on a painting by Benjamin West.

Portuguese conquest of the Banda Orienta.aftermath: At the end of the Portuguese invasion, over 4000 Uruguayans (6% of the entire population of the Banda Oriental) had been killed by the invaders in three and a half years of bloody war.

Quasi-War.outcome: Inconclusive; Convention of 1800 (Treaty of Mortefontaine) restores normal relations.
Quasi-War.aftermath: A two-year undeclared naval war between the US and revolutionary France over US neutrality and the XYZ Affair. The Convention of 1800 ended the alliance of 1778 and laid groundwork for the Louisiana Purchase three years later.

Queen Anne's War.outcome: Peace of Utrecht, Treaty of Portsmouth
Queen Anne's War.aftermath:
Acadia and Newfoundland
Shortly after the war, the French established the Fortress of Louisbourg. The fortified settlement was located to the north of the ceded Acadian territory, on Cape Breton Island.
The loss of Newfoundland and Acadia restricted the French presence on the Atlantic to Île-Saint-Jean (now Prince Edward Island) and Île-Royale (now Cape Breton Island). French were resettled there from Newfoundland, and France constructed the Fortress of Louisbourg in the following years. This presence plus the rights to use the Newfoundland shore resulted in continued friction between French and British fishing interests, which was not fully resolved until late in the 18th century.

Ragamuffin War.aftermath: The Brazilian Army reorganized itself to be a proper fighting force during the Ragamuffin War. The military defeated insurgencies that rose up during the Imperial Era of Brazil. However, this reformed military would prove disastrous against the Emperor when they rebelled to create a Republic.

Reconquista.aftermath: Since the 19th century, traditional Western and especially Iberian historiography has stressed the existence of the Reconquista, a continual phenomenon by which the Christian Iberian kingdoms opposed and conquered the Muslim kingdoms, understood as a common enemy who had militarily seized territory from native Iberian Christians. The concept has served the idea "that Spain is a nation shaped against Islam", contributing to "a largely biased and distorted vision of the Iberian medieval past, aimed at delegitimizing the Islamic presence (al-Andalus) and therefore at legitimizing the Christian conquest of the Muslim territory." Among other arguments, one of those advanced by scholars is that "no military campaign lasts eight centuries.
Reconquista.outcome: Christian victory. Granada surrenders, completing the seven-century reconquest of Iberia.

Reform War.aftermath: A French invasion and the establishment of the Second Mexican Empire followed almost immediately after the end of the Reform War, and key figures of the war would continue to play roles during its rise and fall.
Reform War.outcome: Liberal victory; Benito Juárez restored to the presidency, 1861.

Rus'–Cuman wars.aftermath: A century and a half of intermittent steppe-Slavic conflict. The Cuman confederations dominated the Pontic steppe until both Cumans and Rus principalities were overrun by the Mongol invasions of 1237-1240.

Russian Civil War.aftermath:
upright=1.2|A map of Europe in 1923 after the revolutions of 1917–1923
With the end of the war, the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) no longer faced an acute military threat to its existence and power. However, the perceived threat of continued popular discontent, combined with the failure of socialist revolutions in other countries, such as the German revolution of 1918–1919, contributed to the continued militarization of Soviet society.
Russian Civil War.outcome: Bolshevik (Red) victory. White armies driven from European Russia, then the Far East.

Russian invasion of Ukraine.outcome: Ongoing as of mid-2026. The full-scale invasion began before dawn on 24 February 2022 with cruise missile strikes across Ukraine and ground crossings from Belarus, Russia, and Crimea.
Russian invasion of Ukraine.aftermath: The initial Russian plan to seize Kyiv and decapitate the government within 72 hours failed at Hostomel and along the highways north of the capital. By April 2022 Russian forces had withdrawn from northern Ukraine and shifted focus to the Donbas and the southern land bridge to Crimea. The war has produced the largest tank engagements, drone campaigns, and urban sieges in Europe since 1945. Estimated casualties exceed 500,000 across both sides. The Wagner Group's June 2023 mutiny was a domestic political consequence. Prigozhin died two months later in a plane crash widely attributed to the Kremlin.
Russian invasion of Ukraine.keyTerms: No peace treaty. The Black Sea Grain Initiative (July 2022 to July 2023) was the most significant negotiated agreement before its Russian withdrawal.
notable: Failed Russian offensive on Kyiv ends the initial war plan
Annexation referenda in four Ukrainian oblasts (September 2022), unrecognized internationally
Wagner Group mutiny and march on Moscow (June 2023)
Ukrainian incursion into Kursk Oblast (August 2024), the first foreign occupation of Russian territory since World War II
Tactical innovations: FPV drones, naval drones, Storm Shadow and ATACMS strikes into occupied territory

Russo-Georgian War.aftermath: Russian forces stayed in South Ossetia after the conflict, including at the Java base (pictured)

Russo-Japanese War.aftermath: The first modern war in which an Asian power defeated a European one. Russia's defeat exposed Romanov rot and helped trigger the 1905 revolution. Japan emerged as a great power, paving the way to its conquest of Korea (1910) and Manchuria (1931).

Russo-Persian War (1804–1813).aftermath: Nine years of war that gave Russia control of most of the Caucasus south of the Caucasus mountains. The Treaty of Gulistan transferred Daghestan, Georgia, most of Azerbaijan, and parts of Armenia from Iran to Russia — the foundation of Russian Caucasian hegemony.

Russo-Persian War (1826–1828).aftermath:
Signing ceremony of the Treaty of Turkmenchay
On 2 February 1828, Abbas Mirza signed the Treaty of Turkmenchay, thus ceding Erivan and Nakhichevan as well as agreeing to significant war reparations and other concessions. The province of Azerbaijan and Abbas Mirza's personal fortune provided the majority of the money needed to pay for this. a minor portion came from the British, but none from the shah. Russia was able to put pressure on Iran because of the reparations obligation. The treaty also gave Russia an opportunity to get involved in Iranian politics, as the shah now required Russia's acknowledgment of the person he wanted to name as heir apparent.
Russo-Persian War (1826–1828).outcome: Russian victory; Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828) cedes Iranian Armenia and the Erivan Khanate.

Russo-Swedish War (1788–1790).aftermath:
Memorial of the Battle of Uttismalm erected in Utti, Finland (1931)
The Russo-Swedish War of 1788–1790 was, overall, mostly insignificant for the parties involved. Catherine II regarded the war against her Swedish cousin as a substantial distraction, as her land troops were tied up in the war against Turkey, and she was likewise concerned with revolutionary events unfolding in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (the Constitution of 3 May 1791) and in France (the French Revolution). The Swedish attack foiled the Russian plans of sending its navy into the Mediterranean Sea to support its forces fighting the Ottomans, as it was needed to protect the capital, Saint Petersburg.
Russo-Swedish War (1788–1790).outcome: Inconclusive; Treaty of Värälä (1790) restores status quo ante bellum.

Russo-Turkish War (1768–1774).outcome: Russian victory Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca}}
Russo-Turkish War (1768–1774).aftermath: A six-year war (1768-1774) that confirmed Russian dominance on the Black Sea. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca opened the Black Sea to Russian shipping, gave Russia a protective role over Ottoman Christian subjects, and made the Crimean Khanate nominally independent — a prelude to annexation a decade later.

Russo-Turkish War (1787–1792).aftermath: Accordingly, the Treaty of Jassy was signed on 9 January 1792, recognizing Russia's 1783 annexation of the Crimean Khanate. Yedisan (Odessa and Ochakov) was also ceded to Russia, and the Dniester was made the Russian frontier in Europe, while the Russian Asiatic frontier, the Kuban River, remained unchanged. The Ottoman war goal to reclaim the Crimea had failed, and if not for the French Revolution, the Ottoman Empire's situation could have been much worse.

Russo-Turkish War (1806–1812).aftermath: Although there are sources that describe the war as a Russian victory. there are some that call it indecisive, because the treaty, favourable to the Ottomans, stipulated that Russia returned all occupied lands other than Bessarabia.

Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878).aftermath:
Europe after the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and the territorial and political rearrangement of the Balkan Peninsula.
Under pressure from the British, Russia accepted the truce offered by the Ottoman Empire on 31 January 1878, but continued to move towards Constantinople.
Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878).keyTerms: Treaty of San Stefano (March 3, 1878); Treaty of Berlin (July 13, 1878)

Russo-Ukrainian War.outcome: Ongoing as of mid-2026. No internationally recognized resolution. The full-scale Russian invasion began 24 February 2022.
Russo-Ukrainian War.aftermath: Hundreds of thousands of casualties on both sides. Several million Ukrainians displaced as refugees across Europe. NATO expanded to include Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024). Western sanctions reshaped European energy markets. The war is the largest in Europe since 1945 and remains undetermined.
Russo-Ukrainian War.keyTerms: No treaty. Ceasefires and exchanges have been local and partial.
notable: Largest interstate war in Europe since 1945
NATO expansion to include Finland and Sweden
European energy market restructured away from Russian gas
ICC arrest warrant issued for Vladimir Putin (March 2023)

Rákóczi's War of Independence.aftermath: Eight years of Hungarian revolt against Habsburg rule (1703-1711) led by Francis II Rákóczi. The Peace of Szatmár (1711) restored Habsburg authority but confirmed Hungarian constitutional and religious freedoms — establishing the constitutional framework that lasted until 1848.

Saint-Domingue expedition.aftermath: The expedition resulted with France losing more troops in Saint-Domingue than during the later Battle of Waterloo. Little more than 7,000 to 8,000 of the 31,000 soldiers sent to Saint-Domingue survived and over 20 French generals died. On 1 January 1804 Dessalines proclaimed the colony of Saint-Domingue to be the second independent state in the Americas, under the name of Haiti, and was first made governor general for life before (on 6 October 1804) being crowned emperor as Jacques I. Over 3,000 whites, including women and children, were killed under his supervision in the 1804 Haiti Massacre. He followed a system of "caporalisme agraire" or serfdom that did not include slavery per se but was still aimed at maintaining sugar industry profits by force.

Saxon revolt of 1077–1088.aftermath: Eleven years of revolt by the German nobility against Henry IV during the Investiture Controversy. Henry's eventual restoration was hollow — his son Henry V deposed him in 1105 and the Concordat of Worms (1122) settled the investiture issue.

Scanian War.aftermath: The exact result of the war is disagreed upon by scholars. Some sources view the war as a Swedish defeat, with other sources viewing the war as inconclusive. Historian Michael Fredholm von Essen also claims that one could argue that the real winner of the Scanian war was the French king, Louis XIV, along with Brandenburg. The result of the war and the terms of the peace treaties were a large disappointment for Denmark, being referred to as "En skiden og skammelig fred" ("A lousy and shameful peace") by a priest in Copenhagen.
Scanian War.outcome: Status quo ante bellum; Treaty of Lund (1679).

Second Anglo-Afghan War.aftermath: With Ayub Khan defeated, the war was officially over with Abdur Rahman Khan ruling as Amir, he was seen as the real victor of the Second Anglo-Afghan War. Despite attempts by the British to hold on to Kandahar, they decided to return it to Afghanistan. Rahman confirmed the Treaty of Gandamak, whereby the British took control of the territories ceded by Yaqub Khan. The provocative policy of maintaining a British resident in Kabul was abandoned, but instead British Indian Muslim agents were to be left to smooth liaison between the governments. Britain would also handle Afghanistan's foreign policy in exchange for protection and a subsidy. The Afghan tribes maintained internal rule and local customs, and provided a continuing buffer between the British Raj and the Russian Empire.

Second Anglo-Dutch War.aftermath:
Treaty of Breda
upright=1.7|The conclusion of the Treaty of Breda, at Breda Castle
On 31 July 1667, what is generally known as the Treaty of Breda concluded peace between England and the Netherlands. Under normal cirumstances the Dutch victory in the Medway would probably have been followed by new demands, but the large scale French invasion of the Spanish Netherlands meant that the English came off lightly. Fears of growing French power meant that Johan de Witt and many of his fellow Dutch regenten preferred a quick end to the war with the English.
Second Anglo-Dutch War.keyTerms: Raid on the Medway (June 1667); Treaty of Breda (1667)

Second Anglo-Maratha War.keyTerms: Battle of Assaye (September 23, 1803); Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (December 1803)
Second Anglo-Maratha War.aftermath: A two-year war (1803-1805) in which the East India Company under Arthur Wellesley defeated the major Maratha confederate states. The treaties placed most Maratha territory under British paramountcy; only the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-1818) remained before British power in India was unchallenged.

Second Anglo-Mysore War.aftermath: It was the second of four Anglo-Mysore Wars, which ultimately ended with British control over most of southern India. Pursuant to the terms of the Treaty of Mangalore, the British did not participate in the conflict between Mysore and its neighbours, the Maratha Empire and the Nizam of Hyderabad, that began in 1785. In Parliament, the Pitt administration passed Pitt's India Act that gave the government control of the East India Company in political matters.

Second Anglo-Sikh War.aftermath:
Photograph of captured Sikh guns parked in Ambala cantonment in the aftermath of the Second Anglo-Sikh War, by John McCosh, circa April 1849
Lord Dalhousie proclaimed Britain's annexation of the Punjab on 2 April 1849. His foreign secretary, Henry Meirs Elliot, arrived at Lahore to obtain the signatures of the members of the Council of Regency and Duleep Singh. A durbar was held in the Lahore Fort where Singh affixed his signatures to the document which confirmed the annexation. The Sikh defeat had several causes. Their administration of the population of the Punjab had been poor, which meant that their large armies found it difficult to find enough food while the East India Company had brought overwhelming force against them.
Second Anglo-Sikh War.outcome: British victory; annexation of the Punjab (March 1849).

Second Balkan War.aftermath: The Second Balkan War made Serbia the most militarily powerful state south of the Danube. Years of military investment financed by French loans borne fruit. Central Vardar and the eastern half of the Sanjak of Novi Pazar were acquired. Its territory grew in extent from 18,650 to 33,891 square miles, and its population grew by more than one and a half million. The aftermath brought harassment and oppression for those in the newly conquered lands. The freedom of association, assembly and the press guaranteed under the Serbian constitution of 1903 was not introduced into the new territories.
Second Balkan War.outcome: Romanian-Greek-Serbian-Ottoman victory over Bulgaria; Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913).

Second Banda Oriental campaign.aftermath: See Cisplatine War. The 1816-1820 Portuguese campaign incorporated the Banda Oriental into the Brazilian empire as the Cisplatine Province until Uruguay's independence in 1828.

Second Boer War.aftermath: Three years of war in which Britain deployed 450,000 men against the Boer republics and ended up holding the Transvaal and Orange Free State through a campaign of farm-burning and concentration camps that killed 28,000 Boer civilians and 14,000 Black Africans. The brutality of the war shaped post-war South African politics and gave reformers the case for early-20th-century reform.

Second Crusade.aftermath: The Crusaders were victorious in the west, where they conquered several territories, including Lisbon, which would later become the capital of Portugal and thus the Portuguese Empire. In the east, each of the Christian forces felt betrayed by the other. A plan was made to attack Ascalon, and Conrad took his troops there, but no further help arrived, due to the lack of trust that had resulted from the failed siege. This mutual distrust would linger for a generation, to the ruin of the Christian kingdoms in the Holy Land. After quitting Ascalon, Conrad returned to Constantinople to further his alliance with Manuel. Louis remained behind in Jerusalem until 1149. The discord also extended to the marriage of Louis and Eleanor, which had been falling apart during the course of the crusade.

Second English Civil War.aftermath: Following Charles's execution, the Commonwealth of England was established. In Scotland, Charles II became the new king, the resulting tensions leading to the Anglo-Scottish War of 1650 to 1652.

Second Fitna.aftermath:
First Umayyad gold alt=Coin with protruded inscription in Arabic and a bearded man standing with sheathed sword, seen face-on
With the victory of Abd al-Malik, Umayyad authority was restored and hereditary rule in the caliphate was solidified. Abd al-Malik and his descendants, in two cases his nephews, ruled for another fifty-eight years, before being overthrown by the Abbasid Revolution in 750.
Second Fitna.outcome: Umayyad victory; Abd al-Malik consolidates the caliphate by 692.

Second French intervention in Mexico.aftermath: The republican victory transformed Mexico’s political landscape. The defeat of the French consolidated liberal hegemony and allowed central elites, now organized within the Liberal Party, to impose a state-building project over regional and peripheral powers. in spite of a constitutional prohibition of re-elections.

Second Italian War of Independence.aftermath: A two-month Franco-Sardinian war against Austria in 1859 that produced Italian unification. The Battle of Solferino (with its 40,000 casualties) inspired Henri Dunant to found the Red Cross. The Treaty of Zürich transferred Lombardy from Austria to Sardinia-Piedmont.

Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.aftermath:
Armenia
Protests in Yerevan against the terms of a cease-fire agreement on 18 November 2020.
Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.outcome: Azerbaijani victory; November 2020 ceasefire returns most of the Karabakh region to Azerbaijani control.

Second Opium War.aftermath: Qing flag seized by Anglo-French forces. The flag reads "親兵第五隊右營": Bodyguard, fifth squadron, right battalion (unit types are approximate), Les Invalides.
Second Opium War.keyTerms: Treaty of Tientsin (June 26, 1858); Convention of Peking (October 24, 1860)

Second Punic War.keyTerms: Battle of Cannae (216 BC); Battle of Zama (October 202 BC)
Second Punic War.aftermath: Seventeen years (218-201 BC) of war between Rome and Carthage. Hannibal's invasion of Italy via the Alps produced the catastrophic Roman defeat at Cannae (216 BC), but Roman manpower endured. Scipio's African invasion forced Hannibal's recall; Zama (202 BC) ended the war. Rome became the Mediterranean hegemon.

Second Schleswig War.aftermath:
Austrian veterans from the Second Schleswig War of 1864. photograph taken in 1914 from an excursion they took to Vejle in Denmark the same year.
In the Prussian forces' first clash of arms since reorganization, their effectiveness proved clear, something the Austrians ignored to their cost 18 months later in the Austro-Prussian War, and contributed to a perception in the German states that Prussia was the only state that could defend the other German states against external aggression. (See Unification of Germany.) Prussia and Austria took over the respective administration of Schleswig and Holstein under the Gastein Convention of 14 August 1865. About 200,000 Danes came under German rule.

Second Seminole War.outcome: Nominal end to conflict. no peace treaty. approximately 4,000 Seminoles forcibly transported to Indian Territory. approximately 575 Seminoles remained in Florida. unresolved conflict led to Third Seminole War in 1855.
Second Seminole War.aftermath: Peace had come to Florida for a while. The Natives were mostly staying on the reservation, but there were minor clashes. The Florida authorities continued to press for removal of all Natives from Florida. The Natives tried to limit their contacts with the American settlers as much as possible.

Second Sino-Japanese War.aftermath:
Resumption of the Chinese Civil War
Chiang Kai-shek and Mao Zedong in 1945
Second Sino-Japanese War.outcome: Japanese surrender ends fighting in China August–September 1945.

Second War of Scottish Independence.aftermath: Two decades of war (1332-1357) over the deposed Edward Balliol's English-backed claim to the Scottish throne. The Treaty of Berwick (1357) ransomed David II of Scotland but the war's tactical innovations (English longbow, defensive positions at Halidon Hill, Neville's Cross) shaped the early Hundred Years' War.

Second War of the Diadochi.aftermath: The war had shifted the balance of power to such a degree that Antigonus could pose a threat to any or all of the other Diadochi. this led to Cassander, Ptolemy (with Seleucus) and Lysimachus allying against him in the Third War of the Diadochi. The territories now controlled by Antigonus would later form the basis of the Seleucid Empire.
Second War of the Diadochi.outcome: Antigonid victory in this round; the wars continued for another two decades.

Sicilian Wars.aftermath: Three centuries of intermittent war between Greek Sicily (led by Syracuse) and Carthage. The wars ended only with the Roman conquest of Sicily in the First Punic War, ending the long Greek-Phoenician rivalry on the island.

Siege of Osaka.aftermath: One of the oldest kawaraban newsprints sold during the Edo period, depicting the fall of Osaka Castle

Sino-French War.aftermath:
Political situation
The French Tonkin commemorative medal commemorates several battles of the Sino-French War.
French soldiers in Tonkin, c. 1890

Sino-Vietnamese War.aftermath: China and Vietnam each lost thousands of troops, and China lost 3.45 billion yuan in overhead, which delayed completion of their 1979–80 economic plan. Following the war, the Vietnamese leadership took various repressive measures to deal with the problem of real or potential collaboration. In the spring of 1979, the authorities expelled approximately 8,000 Hoa people from Hanoi to the southern "New Economic Zones", and partially resettled the Hmong tribes and other ethnic minorities from the northernmost provinces. In response to the defection of Hoàng Văn Hoan, the Communist Party of Vietnam removed from its ranks pro-Chinese elements and persons who had surrendered to the advancing Chinese troops during the war. In 1979, a total of 20,468 members were expelled from the party.
Sino-Vietnamese War.outcome: Chinese strategic withdrawal after three weeks; both sides claimed victory.

Soviet–Afghan War.aftermath: Sources consistently characterize the Soviet–Afghan War as a political defeat for the Soviet Union, with some sources also defining the war as a military defeat for the Soviets. Modern literature is divided, with other sources also calling the war a political defeat for the Soviets, but a military draw.

Soviet–Japanese border conflicts.aftermath: A five-year period (1932-1939) of undeclared border war along the Manchukuo borders with the USSR and Mongolian People's Republic. The Soviet victory at Khalkhin Gol (August 1939) under Zhukov decisively influenced Japan's decision to pursue southern (Pacific) rather than northern (Siberian) expansion.

Spanish Civil War.aftermath: Tribute and plaque in memory of murdered or persecuted teachers, Navarre, 1936 and later
Spanish Civil War.outcome: Nationalist victory under Francisco Franco; Republic falls April 1939.

Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire.aftermath: Two years (1519-1521) in which Hernán Cortés, a small Spanish force, and a coalition of native polities led by Tlaxcala destroyed the Aztec Triple Alliance. The Siege of Tenochtitlán (May-August 1521) ended with the destruction of the Aztec capital; Mexico City was built on its rubble. Smallpox epidemics killed at least half the population.

Spanish–American War.aftermath: The war lasted 16 weeks. John Hay (the U.S. ambassador in London) boasted that it had been "a splendid little war". The press showed Northerners and Southerners, blacks and whites fighting against a common foe, helping to ease the scars left from the American Civil War. Exemplary of this was that four former Confederate States Army generals had served in the war, now in the U.S. Army and all of them again carrying similar ranks. These officers were Matthew Butler, Fitzhugh Lee, Thomas L.
Spanish–American War.outcome: US victory; Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines transfer from Spain.

Swabian War.aftermath: A short 1499 war between the Old Swiss Confederacy and the Habsburg Swabian League. The Treaty of Basel formally separated Switzerland from the Holy Roman Empire — a milestone toward Swiss independence formalised at Westphalia 150 years later.

Swedish War of Liberation.aftermath: The resolution of old issues was finally achieved through the understanding between Gustav Vasa and Christian III, which led to a 25-year period of peace during their reigns.

Swedish invasion of Russia.aftermath: The consequences of the failed invasion were far-reaching. The Swedish Empire never added new territory after the Battle of Poltava, and shortly thereafter lost more possessions. George I of Great Britain led Great Britain and Prussia into war against Sweden, and Denmark reentered the war. Russia maintained its conquered possessions in Ingria and the Baltic, was able to consolidate its hold over Ukraine and Poland, develop the new city of Saint Petersburg, and gain vital trade links in the Baltic trade. During the invasion, no less than 20,000 Swedish soldiers and thousands more civilians fell into Russian captivity.

Taiping Rebellion.outcome: Qing victory. The Heavenly Kingdom is crushed at Nanjing in 1864 after fourteen years of war.
Taiping Rebellion.aftermath: Estimated 20 to 30 million dead across south-central China, mostly from famine and disease in the aftermath of the campaigns. The Qing dynasty survived but was structurally weakened. regional armies under Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang outgrew imperial control, foreshadowing the warlord era. The Yangtze basin took a generation to repopulate.

Texas Revolution.aftermath:
Military
When Mexican authorities received word of Santa Anna's defeat at San Jacinto, flags across the country were lowered to half staff and draped in mourning. Denouncing any agreements signed by Santa Anna, a prisoner of war, the Mexican authorities refused to recognize the Republic of Texas. Filisola was derided for leading the retreat and quickly replaced by Urrea. Within months, Urrea gathered 6,000 troops in Matamoros, poised to reconquer Texas. However, the renewed Mexican invasion of Texas never materialized as Urrea's army was redirected to address continued federalist rebellions in other state regions in Mexico.

Third Anglo-Mysore War.aftermath: A fourth and final war was fought between the British and Mysore in 1799, in which Seringapatam was taken, and Tipu was killed in its defence. The victors, rather than partitioning the country, forced Tipu's family into exile and restored control of Mysore to the Wadiyars.

Third Italian War of Independence.aftermath:
Victor Emmanuel II in Venice
In late July 1866, after the Prussian victory over Austria, the Armistice of Nikolsburg ended the hostilities between the two countries, provided that Italy obtained Venetia. The Italian army had advanced to the Isonzo River, the Austrians withdrew and left Venice to Italian hands. Following the Austro-Prussian armistice, France and Prussia pressured Italy to conclude an armistice on its own with Austria. The Italian Prime Minister Bettino Ricasoli initially refused the call and insisted to obtain "natural" frontiers for Italy, including the cession of Venetia and South Tyrol and that Italian interests in Istria were respected.

Third Mithridatic War.keyTerms: Battle of the Lycus (66 BC); Pompey's Eastern Settlement (63 BC)
Third Mithridatic War.aftermath: Eleven years (73-63 BC) of war by which Rome destroyed the Pontic kingdom and brought Asia Minor, Syria, and Judea under direct Roman control. Pompey's eastern settlement reshaped the Roman empire — and provided the wealth and military prestige that fed his rivalry with Caesar a decade later.

Third Punic War.aftermath: alt= a colour photograph of the remains today of part of ancient Carthage |
Third Punic War.outcome: Roman victory; Carthage destroyed and the site salted (146 BC).

Third Servile War.aftermath:
The Fall of Spartacus
The rebels of the Third Servile War were annihilated by Crassus. Pompey's forces did not directly engage Spartacus's forces but his legions moving from the north were able to chase down some 5,000 rebels fleeing the battle, "all of whom he slew". After this action, Pompey sent a dispatch to the Senate, saying that while Crassus certainly had conquered the slaves in open battle, he, Pompey, had ended the war, thus claiming a large portion of the credit and earning the enmity of Crassus. While most of the rebel slaves were killed on the battlefield, some 6,000 survivors were captured by the legions of Crassus, all of whom were crucified along the Appian Way from Rome to Capua.

Third Silesian War.outcome: Prussian survival; status quo ante bellum confirmed at the Treaty of Hubertusburg (1763).
Third Silesian War.aftermath: The Central European theatre of the Seven Years' War. Frederick the Great held off Austria, France, Russia, Sweden, and Saxony for seven years. Prussia survived bankrupt and depopulated but retained Silesia and emerged a great power.

Thirty Years' War.aftermath: Eight million dead. Germany was depopulated for a generation in many regions. The Westphalian principle — that states answer to no higher authority within their borders — became the bedrock of modern international order.

Tonkin campaign.aftermath: A two-year war (1883-1885) by which France conquered Tonkin (northern Vietnam) and broke the Vietnamese tributary relationship with Qing China. The Treaty of Tientsin (June 1885) confirmed the French protectorate and incorporated Tonkin into French Indochina.

Torstenson War.aftermath:
The Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645. Brown: Denmark–Norway. Green: Sweden. Yellow: the provinces of Jämtland and Härjedalen plus Idre and Särna, and the Baltic Sea islands of Gotland and Ösel, which were ceded to Sweden. Red: the province of Halland, ceded for 30 years
Christian's Danish forces were so exhausted that he was forced to accept the mediation of France and the United Provinces in suing for peace. The Peace of Brömsebro was signed on 13 August 1645, a humiliating disaster to Denmark–Norway. The Swedes were exempted from the Sound Dues, the toll for passing through Danish territory into the Baltic Sea.

Toyota War.outcome: Chadian victory; Libyan withdrawal from the Aouzou Strip 1987.
Toyota War.aftermath: A year of mobile desert warfare in 1987 in which Chadian forces — fighting from Toyota pickup trucks — drove the Libyan army out of northern Chad. ICJ ruling (1994) confirmed Chadian sovereignty over the Aouzou Strip.

Uganda–Tanzania War.aftermath:
Analyses
Sociologist Ronald Aminzade asserted that "the key" to Tanzania's victory was its ideological framing of the war as a threat to the nation, thus facilitating the mobilisation of a popular militia that performed well in combat. Aminzade stated that in contrast Uganda "embarked on a nonideological territorial war", deploying forces that suffered from low morale and internal dissension. Journalist Godwin Matatu reasoned that the Uganda Army's failures rested on its low morale and reliance on vehicles and roads which made them vulnerable to Tanzanian ground forces, who travelled on foot for much of the war.
Uganda–Tanzania War.outcome: Tanzanian-UNLF victory; Idi Amin's government falls April 1979.

Ukrainian–Soviet War.outcome: First: Ukraine and Central Powers victory, Second: Soviet victory
Ukrainian–Soviet War.aftermath:
Eastern Europe after the Treaty of Riga
The end of the war saw the incorporation of most of the territories of Ukraine into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic which, on December 30, 1922, was one of the founding members of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). Parts of Western Ukraine fell under the control of the Second Polish Republic, as laid out in the Peace of Riga. The UNR government, led by Symon Petlura, was forced into exile.

Venezuelan War of Independence.aftermath: The Spanish sent a fleet in 1823 to reconquer the country but were defeated at the Battle of Lake Maracaibo. In the following years Venezuelan forces, as part of the army of Gran Colombia, continued campaigning under the leadership of Bolívar to liberate the southern parts of New Granada and Ecuador. Once this was accomplished, Gran Colombia continued its fight against the Spanish in Peru and Bolivia, completing the efforts of Chilean and Argentine patriots, such as José de San Martín, who liberated southern South America.

Vietnam War.outcome: Fall of Saigon (30 April 1975) to North Vietnamese forces. North Vietnam, the Viet Cong, and their allies won.
Vietnam War.aftermath: Vietnam was unified under the communist government in Hanoi as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (1976). ~1 to 3 million Vietnamese died across two decades of war, plus ~58,000 American service members and significant losses in Laos and Cambodia. The Khmer Rouge took Cambodia in the same months and went on to kill ~1.5 to 2 million Cambodians. United States military and political confidence was deeply shaken, with effects on American foreign policy for a generation.
Vietnam War.keyTerms: Paris Peace Accords (27 January 1973) ended direct American involvement. The war between North and South Vietnam continued until Saigon fell on 30 April 1975 without a final treaty.
notable: Unification of Vietnam under the Hanoi government
Cambodian genocide under the Khmer Rouge (1975 to 1979)
Boat people exodus of refugees from Indochina
Lasting effect on American politics and military doctrine

War against the Islamic State.outcome: Coalition victory. The territorial caliphate declared by Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi in Mosul in June 2014 was destroyed by March 2019 with the fall of Baghouz, Syria. The organization persists as an insurgency and franchise.
War against the Islamic State.aftermath: Over five years of intense urban warfare reshaped Mosul, Raqqa, Fallujah, Ramadi, Tikrit, and other cities. The Syrian Democratic Forces, led by the Kurdish YPG, emerged as a US partner that strained the US–Turkey relationship for years after. Tens of thousands of civilians and combatants died. the displacement was on the scale of millions across Iraq and Syria. Baghdadi died in a US raid in Idlib (October 2019). ISIS affiliates remain active in West Africa, the Sahel, Afghanistan-Pakistan (ISIS-K), and elsewhere.
War against the Islamic State.keyTerms: No treaty. The end of the territorial caliphate was declared after the fall of Baghouz on 23 March 2019.
notable: Fall of Mosul to ISIS and the proclamation of the caliphate (June 2014)
Battles of Kobani (2014–2015) and the rise of the SDF
Battle of Mosul (2016–2017) and Battle of Raqqa (2017)
Death of Baghdadi in Idlib (October 2019)
Ongoing insurgency in Syria's Badia and northern Iraq

War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).outcome: Taliban victory. The US-backed Afghan government collapsed on 15 August 2021 as the Taliban entered Kabul. The final American withdrawal completed 30 August 2021.
War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).aftermath: Twenty years and an estimated 176,000 deaths, including ~2,400 US service members and tens of thousands of Afghan security forces and civilians. The United States spent over two trillion dollars. The Taliban reimposed restrictive social policy, particularly affecting women and girls. The departure created a refugee outflow of hundreds of thousands. Al-Qaeda's central leadership was severely degraded over the war but reconstituted in different geographies. ISIS-K emerged as a competitor. NATO's first and longest combat deployment ended without a treaty.
War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).keyTerms: Doha Agreement (29 February 2020) between the United States and the Taliban set the conditions for US withdrawal. No agreement with the Afghan government.
notable: Initial defeat of the Taliban government (October–November 2001)
Battle of Tora Bora and bin Laden's escape (December 2001)
Operation Anaconda (March 2002), first large conventional US ground action
Surge and counterinsurgency strategy (2009–2012)
Fall of Kabul and the Kabul Airport evacuation (August 2021)

War in Iraq (2013–2017).aftermath: Months of relative calm in Baghdad ended with over 27 people killed by suicide bombers over a period of 3 days in mid-January 2018. Although there were no immediate claims of responsibility, it was reported that such attacks had usually been the work of the jihadist group Islamic State (IS) in the past, and that elements of the group were still active north of the city despite the government's claim of victory in December 2017. On Wednesday January 17, two days after the two suicide bombings on January 15, IS "claimed responsibility for the twin suicide bombings in Baghdad this week", though the New York Times suggested that the delay, and a number of errors in the claim, may show that the group's "media apparatus has been disrupted".

War in the Vendée.aftermath: Three years of Catholic-royalist revolt in western France against the revolutionary republic. The republican Infernal Columns (1794) inflicted mass atrocities; total deaths exceeded 170,000. The Vendée remains a contested touchstone in French historical memory, with some scholars characterising the repression as genocidal.

War of 1812.outcome: Treaty of Ghent (24 December 1814) restored the pre-war borders. The war ended in a stalemate, though both sides claimed victory.
War of 1812.aftermath: United States borders with British North America were unchanged. The Battle of New Orleans (8 January 1815) was fought after the treaty was signed but before news reached the parties. Native American confederations in the Northwest and the South lost their most effective resistance to American expansion. Britain shifted its colonial focus toward what would become Canada.
War of 1812.keyTerms: Treaty of Ghent (24 December 1814), restoring status quo ante bellum.
notable: Burning of Washington by British forces (August 1814)
Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans (January 1815)
End of organized Native resistance east of the Mississippi
Beginning of nearly two centuries of unguarded United States to Canada border

War of Jenkins' Ear.aftermath: A nine-year Anglo-Spanish war (1739-1748) merged into the War of the Austrian Succession. The British attack on Cartagena de Indias (1741) failed catastrophically; the war ended at Aix-la-Chapelle with no significant changes to the colonial map.

War of Saint Sabas.outcome: Venetian victory; Genoese expelled from Acre 1258.
War of Saint Sabas.aftermath: Sixteen years of war between the Italian maritime republics over a monastery in Acre. The conflict accelerated the decline of the Crusader states by dividing their commercial sponsors and contributing to Acre's eventual fall in 1291.

War of the Austrian Succession.aftermath: Eight years of war that confirmed Maria Theresa's succession but legitimised Prussia's seizure of Silesia. The war's unresolved tensions led directly to the Seven Years' War a decade later.

War of the Confederation.aftermath: General Bulnes again assumed the initiative. After the defeat of the Confederate army at Yungay on January 20, the Chileans commenced a second push southward, occupying Lima for the second time in April. Santa Cruz had already fled to Ecuador, and both the war and the short-lived Peru-Bolivian Confederation now came to an end.

War of the Fifth Coalition.aftermath:
The Battle of Znaim was the last action between Austria and France in the War of the Fifth Coalition
After the main Austrian force was defeated at Wagram, the nation's forces collapsed, according to historian Charles Esdaile, and Emperor Francis was forced to sue for peace. Englund attributes the end to "diplomatic considerations" and believes that Austria could have continued to fight. The Treaty of Schönbrunn, signed on 14 October 1809, imposed a heavy political toll on the Austrians. Metternich and Charles succeeded in negotiating lighter terms in return for Austrian co-operation and most of the hereditary Habsburg territories were preserved.
War of the Fifth Coalition.keyTerms: Battle of Wagram (July 5-6, 1809); Treaty of Schönbrunn (October 14, 1809)

War of the First Coalition.outcome: French victory. Treaty of The Hague, Treaty of Paris, Peaces of Basel, Treaty of Tolentino, Treaty of Campo Formio
War of the First Coalition.aftermath: Five years of war that saved the Republic from the Allied invasion of 1792, then carried French armies into Italy, the Rhineland, and the Low Countries. Napoleon emerged as the dominant French general at the Italian campaign of 1796-97.

War of the Fourth Coalition.aftermath:
Prussia (orange) and its territories lost at Tilsit (other colours)
Following the Treaties of Tilsit, Britain and Sweden remained the only two major coalition members still at war with France. Russia soon declared war against Britain and after a British attack on Copenhagen, Denmark–Norway joined the war on the side of Napoleon (Gunboat War), opening a second front against Sweden. A short British expedition under Sir John Moore was sent to Sweden (May 1808) to protect against any possible Franco-Danish invasion.
War of the Fourth Coalition.keyTerms: Battle of Friedland (June 14, 1807); Treaty of Tilsit (July 7, 1807)

War of the League of Cambrai.aftermath: The Triumph of Venice (oil on canvas by Pompeo Batoni, 1737) depicts Leonardo Loredan, Doge of Venice during the war.
War of the League of Cambrai.outcome: Venetian survival; the League dissolved by Venetian diplomacy by 1516.

War of the League of Cognac.keyTerms: Sack of Rome (May 6, 1527); Treaty of Cambrai (August 5, 1529)
War of the League of Cognac.outcome: Habsburg victory; Treaty of Cambrai (1529) confirms Habsburg dominance in Italy.
War of the League of Cognac.aftermath: A three-year war by France, Venice, Florence, the Papacy, and Milan against Charles V. The Sack of Rome (May 1527) by mutinying Imperial troops is its most famous moment. The Treaty of Cambrai — the "Ladies' Peace" — was negotiated by Louise of Savoy and Margaret of Austria.

War of the Polish Succession.aftermath: A four-year war (1733-1738) over the Polish throne. France backed Stanisław Leszczyński, Russia and Austria backed Augustus III of Saxony. The Treaty of Vienna (1738) confirmed Augustus on the Polish throne and transferred Lorraine to France (its last major territorial gain in continental Europe before the Revolution).

War of the Portuguese Succession.aftermath: The combined Spanish-Portuguese navy's victory resulted in the rapid conquest of the Azores, completing the dynastic union of the Portuguese and Spanish empires. The King Philip II of Spain was recognized as King Philip I of Portugal and of the Algarves by the Portuguese Cortes of Tomar (1581). In 1589, António made an attempt on Lisbon supported by English forces under the command of Sir Francis Drake and Sir John Norreys. When the people failed to rise and yield the city to Dom António, the attempt was abandoned. Spain and Portugal would remain united in a dynastic union of the crowns (remaining formally independent and with autonomous administrations) for the next 60 years, until 1640. This union is called the Iberian Union.

War of the Pyrenees.outcome: French victory; Peace of Basel (1795) cedes Spanish Santo Domingo to France.
War of the Pyrenees.aftermath: Spain's contribution to the First Coalition ended with the Peace of Basel — Spain not only conceded but switched alliance and joined France against Britain (1796 Treaty of San Ildefonso).

War of the Quadruple Alliance.aftermath: The war provided a unique example during the eighteenth century in which Britain and France were on the same side. It came during a period between 1716 and 1731, when the two countries were allies. Spain would later join with France in the Bourbon Compact, and the two would become enemies of the British once more. Spain later regained the Kingdom of Naples during the 1733 to 1735 War of the Polish Succession.

War of the Second Coalition.aftermath: On 25 March 1802, Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens, ending British involvement in the war. After a preliminary treaty signed at Paris on 9 October 1801, the Treaty of Paris of 25 June 1802 ended the war between France and the Ottoman Empire, the last remaining member of the Second Coalition. The peace treaties ceded the left bank of the Rhine to France and recognized the independence of the Cisalpine, Batavian and Helvetic republics. Thus began the longest period of peace during the period 1792–1815.
War of the Second Coalition.keyTerms: Treaty of Lunéville (February 9, 1801); Peace of Amiens (March 25, 1802)

War of the Sicilian Vespers.outcome: Peace of Caltabellotta, House of Barcelona gains Sicilian throne
